title: Silent Adrenal Pheochromocytoma Coexistent with Corticomedullary Hyperplasia: A Case Incidentally Discovered
central_claims: Rare coexistence of silent pheochromocytoma, corticomedullary hyperplasia and subclinical hypercortisolism; local ACTH is a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated cause.

source_manifest.title: Silent Adrenal Pheochromocytoma Coexistent with Corticomedullary Hyperplasia: A Case Incidentally Discovered
source_manifest.finding: Single histologically characterized case with normal urinary metanephrines, cortisol excess and corticomedullary hyperplasia; ACTH-mediated cortical change proposed, not experimentally established.

source_manifest.title: Silent pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma: Systematic review and proposed definitions for standardized terminology
source_manifest.finding: Review extracts individual-case data from 85 reports and 157 patients. This report is reference 20 within the clinically silent case set (references 14–57). It supports phenotypic characterization, while warning that absence of symptoms or normal biochemical tests does not establish lack of catecholamine synthesis.

source_manifest.title: Adrenal Medullary Hyperplasia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
source_manifest.finding: 66 patients from 29 reports support heterogeneous AMH, but the text does not cite Petramala or establish reuse or replication of this case.

source_manifest.title: A Rare Case: Adrenal Corticomedullary Mixed Tumor With Elements of Pheochromocytoma, Cortical Adenoma, and Ganglioneuroma Cells
source_manifest.finding: Different mixed tumor explicitly distinguished from pheochromocytoma with cortical hyperplasia; cannot reproduce the target combination.

research.summary: The case contributes patient-level evidence to a 2022 independent systematic review. Broader silent-tumor literature is not a replication of its rare combined pathology, and modern terminology cautions against equating silence with absent catecholamine synthesis.
